div.p: m,k)-firm constraints have been used to schedule tasks in soft/firm real-time systems under overloaded conditions. In general, they are provided by application designers to guarantee the minimum levels of quality of service (QoS). Many problems concentrating in task schedulability under these constraints were investigated in the last ten years. However, little work has been done in combining the optimization of the QoS and task schedulability subject to these (m, k)-firm constraints. In this paper, we consider the problem of maximizing the guaranteed performance while maintaining a schedulable task set in periodic firm real-time systems. To quantify the performance, we propose a granularityrelated metric called Granularity of Quality of Service -Reward (GQoS-reward). We then show that maximizing the total GQoS-reward is an NP-Hard problem and a heuristic method to solve the problem is studied. In addition to the improvement to the GQoS, positive effects on other main performance metrics for soft/firm real time systems, such as effective processor utilization (EPU), total accumulated reward and instability, are also supported by the simulation results using our optimization strategy.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Traditionally, many real-time applications are sets of periodic tasks in which each task of a set executes at a fixed rate and has a specific deadline. They are called hard real-time systems since violating task deadlines can be catastrophic. In contrast, a real-time task is considered soft if occasionally missing the task's deadline is not considered a failure and the degree of correctness is determined by how much the deadline has been missed. A firm real-time task is a special case of the soft real time task. For a firm real-time task, only finishing execution by its deadline is considered to be successful. Completion of the tardy task has no value to the real-time system. A number of models have been advocated for firm real-time systems. Examples are Skip-over model [2], Window-constrained model [3] and (m,k)-constrained model [1]. In the (m,k)constrained model, m out of any k consecutive jobs' deadlines must be met. This model is more realistic for capturing the temporal requirements of firm periodic tasks thanks to the incorporation of granularities of quality. It is also the generalization of classic hard and firm periodic real-time tasks. For instance, (1,1)constrained represents the hard real time requirement and (2,3)-constrained designates at most one deadline can be missed in any three consecutive job releases. The (m,k)-constrained model also can increase the schedulability of tasks set under overloaded conditions. Since it doesn't have to require all jobs to meet their deadlines, the system may be schedulable under this constraint while otherwise it is not. In most applications using (m,k) constraints, the notion of (m,k) represents a quality of guaranteed service metric: the more m out of any k consecutive jobs meet their deadlines, the better the quality produced by the application/task.

To exploit the (m,k)-constrained model, several static and dynamic techniques have been proposed. For dynamic methods, Hamdaoui and Ramanathan [1] present a best-effort scheduling algorithm which raises the priority of jobs that are going to violate their (m,k)constraints. However, it cannot guarantee that these constraints are satisfied. For static methods, to assure the deterministic firm real time requirements, a specific pattern is used to partition jobs in each task as mandatory and optional. Mandatory jobs have their own original priority and all optional jobs are assigned the lowest priority. The pattern is repeated within an infinite sequence of jobs. Although static methods can use the pattern to perform a schedulability test for the task set and then assure the minimum required granularity levels of QoS, there is a gap between this lower bound and the total maximum across the system. This is because (m,k)-constraints are usually designated by the computing modules (tasks) designers. In the design stage, they only care about the acceptable levels of application performance and actually do not take the issues of task scheduling into their considerations. Hence, it is impossible that the computation resource (e.g., CPU time) is just used up for the mandatory jobs (guaranteed granularity of QoS) without looking into the schedulability stage. Although optional jobs can be run when no mandatory job executes or waits, the guaranteed QoS is hardly maximized because of the lack of investigation about the interactions among the (m,k) constraints, task schedulability, and performance.

There have been several papers related to task scheduling and system performance. Periods' selection is discussed in [5,6] as an off-line design aid for choosing the optimal frequencies' combination of classic periodic task sets. This paper extends our preliminary result in the RTAS 2006 WIP session, and the purpose of the research work is twofold. On one side, to make use of the surplus computing time once the original pre-defined (m,k) constraints have been satisfied, we aim to complete additional important mandatory jobs (thus yielding finer granularity) rather than to run optional jobs. To accomplish it, each task T i associates with a class of finite levels of QoS (e.g., (m, k) OR (m+1, k) OR …… OR (k, k)) and each level in the class has a specific reward value. We call the reward the Granularity of Quality of Service reward (GQoSreward). All of the reward values are assigned according to the relative importance of the guaranteed granularity of service among all tasks within the system. Hence, the objective can be transformed into optimizing the total GQoS-reward. On the other side, since the (m, k)-constrained model is used for overloaded systems, we are also interested in improving the soft/firm realtime system performance under overload. To measure the performance, some metrics have been proposed, such as effective processor utilization (EPU) [13] and instability [15]. Informally, EPU measures the fraction of time spent on executing tasks that complete by their deadlines and instability represents changes of the output quality/benefit produced by the task.

Almost all applications suitable for the (m, k)constrained model would benefit from our strategy, which ensures that the variance of the reward is small over time, achieving a stable QoS. The more stable the QoS, the higher the benefit. In fact, in these applications, using later jobs to recover from previous ones' low rewards may not be desirable. Consider an adaptive optics system from astronomical observatories and surveillance satellites. In this application, light from an astronomical object such as a star and similarly, a ground object such as a car, is distorted by the earth atmosphere. The adaptive optics system employs a high-speed control computer, with an array of digital signal processors, to periodically adjust a deformable (adaptive) lens or mirror based on the periodic input from a wave front sensor. The control task must calculate, a thousand times per second (i.e., period = 1 ms), how much and where to deform the lens or mirror to compensate for atmospheric distortion (i.e., wave front error). The corrected light is then passed through another lens, focusing it into a high-resolution image. It is clear that in this application, QoS stability over time is critical since increasing the reward later following a low-reward interval is definitely not desirable.
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows.

In section 2, we first present the process model. Then, we give a motivational example to illuminate the problems and then formally define the problem. In section 3, we demonstrate our idea for solving the problem. Section 4 contains the experiment results and the analysis on those results. The summary and a discussion of future works are given in the last section.

div.head: Process model
div.p: A task set of n independent periodic tasks is represented as T = {T 1 ,…., T n }. Each task T i is characterized by a 5-tuple {P i , C i , m i , k i , R i } where P i is the period of the task, C i is the worst case execution time (WCET), m i and k i (0 ≤ m i ≤ k i ) define the (m,k) constraint for T i and R i is a reward vector of size k i -m i + 1. Each element in the vector contains one version of GQoS-reward, e.g., the reward for (m i , k i ) level or the reward for the (m i +1, k i ) level, and so on. Without loss of generality, we define the values in R i in the sense of monotonic increasing with their index. In other words, r i(0) is the smallest reward (it is 0 if the original m i is 0) for guaranteeing (m i , k i )-firm deadline, while the last element of the reward vector is the largest for satisfying a hard deadline, (k i, k i ), or (1,1) equivalently. Before running on the system, exactly one version of GQoS for each task is to be determined. In addition to the above definitions, we also assume that the relative deadline of each task is the same as the task's period and all tasks are in phase.

If m i = 0, all jobs of T i are optional similarly); otherwise, it is optional. Quan et al improves the result of [4] in [7]. We use the evenly-distributed-mandatory pattern in our work since it has been reported that it exhibits a relative good schedulability and stability [4,7].

Regarding the scheduling method, we adopt the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) algorithm, a well-known dynamic algorithm that assigns priorities to individual jobs in the tasks according to their absolute deadlines [8,12]. In mandatory/optional job scheduling, the mandatory jobs of each task are assigned the priority according to the EDF algorithm and all optional jobs of every task are assigned the lowest priority. If two or more optional jobs compete for the processor while no mandatory jobs are eligible to run, the one with the earliest deadline executes first. If they happen to same deadline, any arbitrary priority assignment can be used to break the ties.

div.head: Motivation
div.p: In this part, we show that carefully choosing the (m, k) constraint, thus the guaranteed granularity of service for each task, is important to the system's overall performance.

Consider a task set of three tasks with the following parameters: Since the utilization of the task set is 1.10, it is obviously that the task set is not schedulable without using (m, k) constraints. With the help of (m, k) constraints, the schedule of meeting all mandatory jobs' deadline is shown in Figure 1(a). Note that in this case, using either the deeply-red pattern or evenly-distributed pattern produces the same result. It is not difficult to see that all tasks in Figure 1(a) only attain their minimum acceptable QoS, and the total GQoS-reward of the system for this case is 10+20+50 = 80. However, with more in-depth analysis, the total one can be increased by adjusting the (m,k) constraints used at run-time. In fact, for this example, we can increase either m 1 to 2 or m 2 to 2. In both cases, they all raise the total GQoSreward while satisfying the new (m, k)-related rules. For example, Figure 1 In addition to improve the overall granularity of QoS, several interesting phenomenon can be seen in the example. Firstly, one idle interval (form 56 to 60) is left within the schedule in Figure1(a). The EPU of this schedule is the lowest among the three example schedules. This is because some optional job(s) which in fact can be executed as mandatory job(s) have to be blocked by other mandatory jobs, while there has some idle intervals after executing the leftover optional jobs. Another phenomenon is well-known, although it is not reflected from our example: EDF performs very poorly under overload [16]. Secondly, it is not difficult to see that the output produced from the schedule in Figure 1(a) is non-stable. However, after raising the m of k for some task, EPU and output stability are all enhanced for schedules in Figure 1 (b) and Figure 1 (c). As a result of the above observations, we guess our idea has positive effects on those soft/firm real-time performance metrics. The rationale behind our conjecture is that since we reserve as much resource as possible for important mandatory jobs, the space for the source of negative factor, overloaded optional jobs, is compressed. Hence, the maximum degree of the possible degrades is minimized, and then it is very likely that the soft/firm real time performances can be improved.

div.head: Problem definition
div.p: In this section, we are going to define the problem formally. According to the relative importance among all tasks in the task set system, each task T i has a multiversion GQoS rewards. The number of versions in task T i is dependent on the (m i , k i ) parameter and then it equals k i -m i + 1. Our goal is to determine the version of GQoS for each task such that the total GQoS rewards is maximized while satisfying the corresponding (m, k) firm deadline requirements.
Formally, the problem can be defined as:

div.p: The question of how to define the rewards is not independent to our problem. However, it is better to leave the freedom to the system designers. Here, we propose a simple and reasonable method to define the GQoS-rewards and we use it in our experiments: each task is assigned an importance factor, and the GQoSrewards are assigned by which the factor times the corresponding values of m (e.g., the GQoS-rewards for T 1 in the motivational example can be defined as an importance factor 10 times the corresponding values of m in the valid range, which are 1 and 2 for T 1 ). Furthermore, to achieve fairness, the values can be adjusted to avoid putting the "surplus" resource together only into a few tasks.

div.head: GQoS-reward optimization problem
div.p: In this section, we first show that the complexity of the problem being targeted is NP-Hard. Then we demonstrate our technique for solving the problem.

div.head: Complexity issues
div.p: By using patterns where the job of every task is mandatory and has the worst case response time, we can check whether the task set is schedulable for EDF by simulating all mandatory jobs within the first busy interval (the readers are referred to [17] for the detailed description of the schedulability test algorithm). However, the problem of selecting the best version of GQoS for each task, while the total reward is maximized and all mandatory jobs are schedulable is not easy. In fact, it is an NP-Hard problem where the proof can be attained by using the reduction from the 0-1 constrained knapsack maximization problem. The formal proof can be found in the appendix.

div.head: Solving the problem
div.p: If the number of tasks in the task set and the number of versions of each task are not large, an exhaustive search method similar to that in [6] can be used.

Although we are able to use the Branch-and-Bound strategy to soften the work slightly, unfortunately, the number of possible combinations of GQoS increases exponentially with the number of tasks or the total number of granularity versions in all tasks. If the task set has a very large number of tasks, it is impossible to finish the job within a reasonable length of time. Thus, a heuristic solution must be used to solve the problem efficiently.

div.p: Algorithm 1 applying the principle is shown in Figure 2. It works as a greedy algorithm. It always picks the schedulable version of GQoS which has the largest ratio on reward of resource demand. If one version for a task is chosen, the coarser versions for that task are removed from the sorted list and only finer versions are left for try. By accomplishing this process, the "surplus" computing resource are reserved for relative important tasks as much as possible.

div.head: Experimental results
div.p: In this section, we first use simulative experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our heuristic method to solve the GQoS-reward optimization problem, and discover the positive effects of maximizing granularities of QoS.
In the first part, we simulate our heuristic algorithm on the same task sets whose sizes are relatively small. The task sets are divided into 9 groups evenly by their effective utilizations ( ∑
div.formula: i * i i * i P k C m ) from 0.1 -1.0.
div.p: Each group contains at least 100 randomly generated task sets. Then we compare our solution with the optimal solution that is obtained with an exhaustive search. Figure 3 shows the optimal total GQoS-reward and our approximated total GQoS-reward normalized to the initial total GQoS-reward (the granularities of QoS over the system with original (m, k) parameters). It can be seen that our heuristic solutions are very close to the optimal results. Actually, in the experiments, our algorithm finds the optimal solution most of the time. In the second part, we want to find out the relationship between the optimization of the granularities of QoS and the performance of soft/firm real-time system. We adopt some popular soft/firm realtime system performance metrics in the literature such as EPU [13] and instability [15]. In the experiments, 500 task sets are randomly generated. The periods are randomly selected between 10 and 150 and the deadlines are assumed to be equal to their periods. The worst case execution time (WCET) of a task is uniformly distributed from 1 to its deadline. Similar to the experiments in the first part of this section, the task sets are divided into 9 groups according to their effective utilizations. To reduce the statistical errors, we assure that each group contains at least 20 schedulable task sets. To measure EPU and instability, the task sets are simulated within the K-LCMs (Least common multiple of P i * k i ). EPUs are obtained by calculating the fraction of time during the interval that the processor spends on executing tasks that complete by their deadlines. To calculate instabilities, the idea in [15] is used, which sees the instability of a task as a discrete sum of changes on the number of the task completions between any two consecutive distinct intervals. To accommodate the requirements of the (m, k)-constrained model, we define the length of the intervals for a task to be the same as the parameter of k for that task and the intervals are overlapped. We hope that our algorithm improves the soft/firm real-time performance on both EPU and instability. Figure 4 shows the comparison results on EPU. Compared with the results that are not optimized, our proposed technique has significant improvements when the effective utilization of the system is relatively low. As the utilization increases, the improvement decreases because of the space of improvement becomes less available. However, it is very attractive that our strategy always keeps the Avg. EPU around 95%. For instability, an amazing and a very huge improvement can be found in Figure 5. The Avg. instability is maintained at a very low level , and hence, it supports that the simulated systems are very stable in QoS by using our method. In order to discover the effects of our optimization strategy more thoroughly, we also investigate the comparisons on accumulated value (AV) although this metric is not very good for the (m, k)-constrained model since it lacks the enforcement on granularity. We assign each task in the experiment a value and assign the GQoS-rewards according to this value, and then we calculate the total accumulated value that is in the same sense of the total weighted completion count (CC) [13,14]. In our experiments, about 85% of the cases improve the results and the Avg. case by using our technique is slightly better than the case without using it (Table 1). The reason for the small improvement on Avg. is that after we raise the m of k for some relative important tasks, in fact, we raise the priority of some jobs in the tasks by changing them into mandatory. However, since those jobs could be run even if they were optional, but block some other optional jobs after changing them into mandatory, the system may lose accumulated rewards in total for some cases. Nonetheless, while considering this together with other performance perspectives, the enhancement in the overall performance is apparent by using our optimization strategy.

div.head: Summary and future works
div.p: In this paper, with respect to both the guaranteed granularity of QoS and soft/firm real-time performance, we propose a novel performance metric, GQoS-reward, for (m,k)-constrained real-time systems. We show with a motivational example that without carefully selecting the best run-time (m, k) parameter for each task, it is not likely to maximize the total performance which combines the granularities of QoS and the importance of each task. After that, we define the GQoS-reward optimization problem formally and show that it is NPhard. We then present our heuristic solution which approximates the optimal solution very well for solving the problem efficiently. To test our method's

Having achieved exciting and dramatic improvements, we conclude that it is very worthy of selecting the best schedulable versions of granularity of QoS before the (m, k)constrained tasks are run on the system, especially for the case of low effective utilization.
Our future work includes investigating the employment of the (m, k)-constrained model on multiprocessor systems or exploring power-aware computing for (m, k)-constrained real-time systems.

div.head: Appendix
div.p: In this section, we show that maximizing the total GQoS-reward while satisfying the corresponding redefined (m,k)-firm deadline constraints is an NP-Hard problem. To finish the proof, we use a reduction of the 0-1 knapsack problem that has been proved as an NP-Hard problem [11] to our problem .
The 0-1 constrained knapsack problem is defined as:

Given an instance of 0-1 constrained knapsack problem P = { p 1 , p 2 …… p n }, W = { w 1 , w 2 …… w n }, we construct an instance of GQoS-reward maximization problem : each task T i has a worst case execution time e i = w i . The period and relative deadline of each task are all equal to M. The number of granularities of QoS for each task is 2 , represented as (m i , k i ) = (0,1) and (1,1). The reward for the case of (0,1) is trivial, which is 0. On the other side, the reward for the case of (1, 1) for task T i is p i . By view of this point, if x i =1, p i x i means the GQoS-reward of selecting (1, 1)-version of granularity of QoS for T i . Otherwise, (0, 1) is selected instead.

It is not difficult to see that p i x i is maximized in 0-1 constrained knapsack problem if and only if the total GQoS-reward is maximized in the GQoS-reward maximization problem. Since the transformation between the given instance of 0-1 constrained knapsack problem and the instance of GQoS-reward maximization problem is finished in polynomial time, we thus know that GQoS-reward maximization problem is also an NP-Hard problem.
